A2.text:
Oliver is a young lawyer in Baku. His friend Yunus makes beautiful plates in Icherisheher. Oliver wants to speak Azerbaijani well, but he has a strong British accent. He always reads grammar books.

One day, they went to a traditional tea house near the Maiden Tower. Oliver wanted to practice speaking. “I will make small talk with the waiter,” Oliver said.

“Good idea,” Yunus answered. “Do not be shy. Close your books. Use your hands and body language.”

The waiter came to the table. Oliver tried to ask about the delicious local food. But he was very nervous. He did not want to mispronounce the words. Instead of saying “chicken,” he accidentally said “cow” in Azerbaijani. Then he tried to use some street slang he learned on the internet.

The waiter looked confused for a second. Then, he started laughing loudly. “You are a funny guy!” the waiter said in perfect English.

Oliver turned red and hid his face. “I am sorry,” he said.

“Do not worry! Sometimes you just need to get your point across,” Yunus smiled. “He understands that you are very hungry.”

The waiter brought them hot tea and a big plate of fresh food. Oliver's language was not perfect, but they had a great lunch together.

B1.text:
Oliver, an expat lawyer working in Baku, was determined to improve his Azerbaijani. He spent hours studying grammar, but his heavy British accent often made conversations difficult. His best friend Yunus, a talented potter in Icherisheher, always told him to relax and stop worrying about being perfectly bilingual.

On a beautiful, sunny Saturday, they sat at a busy tea house near the Maiden Tower. Oliver closed his notebook. “Today, I will make small talk with the waiter,” he announced bravely.

“Finally!” Yunus laughed. “Remember, you do not need perfect fluency. Just speak your mind and use some body language. People appreciate the effort.”

When the waiter approached, Oliver confidently tried to order a popular local chicken dish. However, he was terrified he would mispronounce the difficult vowels. In his panic, he accidentally asked for a roasted cow. Realising his mistake, Oliver panicked and quickly threw in a bit of Baku slang he had read online to sound more natural.

The waiter stared at him in silence. For a moment, Oliver wanted the ground to open up and swallow him. Then, the waiter burst into loud laughter.

“Roasted cow coming right up!” the waiter replied in excellent English, wiping a tear from his eye.

Oliver covered his face in embarrassment. “That was a disaster. I should just speak English.”

“Not at all,” Yunus said, pouring them both some tea. “Communication is not about perfect grammar. You managed to get your point across, and you made him smile. That is a win.”

Oliver sighed, but soon he was laughing too. When the food arrived, it was exactly what he had wanted. He quickly realised that making mistakes was just part of the journey.

B2.text:
Oliver, a British lawyer who had relocated to Baku two years ago, treated learning Azerbaijani like preparing for a supreme court trial. He memorised thick grammar books and obsessed over vocabulary. Yet, despite his hard work, his harsh accent and lack of natural fluency meant he often struggled in real-life situations.

His close friend Yunus, a potter with a small workshop in the winding streets of Icherisheher, always tried to loosen him up. Yunus was effortlessly bilingual and knew that true connection required more than just textbook precision.

“You overthink it,” Yunus told him one breezy Saturday as they sat outside a traditional tea house near the Maiden Tower. “Stop trying to be flawless. Don’t beat around the bush with formal phrases. Just speak your mind. Use some body language and throw in a bit of local slang. Even if you mispronounce a word, people will love that you are trying.”

Oliver took a deep breath. “Right. I’m going to make small talk with the waiter and order our lunch entirely in Azerbaijani.”

When the elderly waiter approached their table, Oliver puffed out his chest. He intended to ask for a specific regional chicken dish, but the pressure got to him. He completely forgot the standard word and ended up using an obscure rural dialect term he had read about, accidentally demanding a whole roasted sheep instead. Panicking, he tried to recover by using a very casual street greeting he had heard teenagers use at the mall.

The waiter froze, his bushy eyebrows raised high. Oliver braced himself for a scolding. Instead, the old man’s face broke into a massive grin, and he began to laugh so hard he had to hold onto the table.

“A whole sheep for the English gentleman!” the waiter chuckled in flawless English.

Oliver sank into his chair, entirely mortified. “I’m never speaking this language again.”

“Are you joking? That was brilliant,” Yunus laughed, clapping him on the shoulder. “You didn't just get your point across; you made his entire week. That’s what communication is actually about.”

Oliver groaned, but a smile crept onto his face. When their food arrived, it was the best meal they had eaten all month.
